extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, essayists, and students of criticism (especially English literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Norms and practical standards for doing literary criticism: what critics should value, how they should work, the critic's temper and subject‑matter, and how to judge works. Emphasises disinterestedness, erudition, and patience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterested endeavour (definition of criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism is 'a disinterested endeavour to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be motivated by seeking and spreading truth/knowledge, not by partisan, sectarian, or practical interests. The critic's primary duty is to the ideal of the best thought and knowledge rather than to short‑term practical aims or personal affiliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid personal attack and controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should eschew 'all personal attack and controversy' and avoid allowing personal enmities to shape critical remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make criticism a vehicle for personal vendetta or public controversy; criticisms aimed at the work, not the person, and refrain from reprinting or reviving polemical personal attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from the practical spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Criticism must maintain its independence of the practical spirit and its aims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not endorse or refuse works simply because they serve practical, political, or utilitarian ends. A work's practical consequences do not count as a substitute for correctness or intellectual soundness; the critic must be willing to dissent from widely applauded practical movements when they impoverish the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience and the ability to wait
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism 'must be patient, and know how to wait; and flexible, and know how to attach itself to things and how to withdraw from them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the impulse to rush nascent ideas into public/regulatory action; allow ideas to mature. Be prepared to support an idea at one stage and withdraw or modify support as fuller knowledge appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility: attach to and withdraw from things
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism must 'know how to attach itself to things and how to withdraw from them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to praise elements of a work when merited, and to retract or revise judgments when they cease to hold. This requires intellectual flexibility rather than rigid adherence to early positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment beyond practical moral lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must be 'apt to study and praise elements that for the fulness of spiritual perfection are wanted, even though they belong to a power which in the practical sphere may be maleficent' and 'apt to discern the spiritual shortcomings or illusions of powers that in the practical sphere may be beneficent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate qualities within works on their own merits: a practically objectionable institution or movement may contain elements of spiritual or aesthetic value, and vice versa. Example given: finding Catholic marriage theory 'refreshing and elevating' even while critiquing the English Divorce Court's practical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge (fresh learning) as critic's chief concern
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Knowledge, and ever fresh knowledge, must be the critic's great concern for himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic's work should primarily be to acquire and communicate new, high‑quality knowledge to readers. Critical writing that conveys informed, fresh learning is more valuable than mere abstract application of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication first, judgment second
rubrics_metrics.description: By communicating fresh knowledge, 'and letting his own judgment pass along with it — insensibly, and in the second place, not the first, as a sort of companion and clue, not as an abstract lawgiver,' the critic does most good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let facts, contexts, and learned exposition lead; allow evaluative judgments to emerge naturally alongside information rather than dominating the piece as abstract prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When subject is familiar: judgment must avoid abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticism deals with a very familiar subject so that fresh knowledge is out of the question, 'it must be all judgment; an enunciation and detailed application of principles' — but 'never to let oneself become abstract.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comparative or canonical work where new facts are limited, focus on clear concrete applications of principles, grounded in intimate consciousness of the truth of what you say; avoid purely formal, detached dicta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide reading: possess at least one great foreign literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Every critic should try and possess 'one great literature, at least, besides his own; and the more unlike his own, the better.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate deep knowledge of at least one non‑native literary tradition to broaden perspective and avoid provincialism. This foreign literature should contrast substantially with your own to maximize critical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmopolitan erudition (classical and comparative knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism which 'regards Europe as being, for intellectual and spiritual purposes, one great confederation' should be equipped 'with a knowledge of Greek, Roman, and Eastern antiquity, and of one another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue classical and comparative study (languages, antiquity, other national literatures) to place contemporary works in a broader, transnational intellectual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a high ideal and perpetual dissatisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism's duty is 'to be perpetually dissatisfied with these works, while they perpetually fall short of a high and perfect ideal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold literary work against a high, exacting ideal; the critic's role includes reminding authors/readers of what is lacking and of loftier possibilities, even when works have real utility or earnest intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist false popular estimates and indiscriminate praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should 'resist' the 'false estimate' that applauds every work as excellent merely because it is popular or aligned with a movement (example: the inflated praise of Bishop Colenso's book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be swayed by current enthusiasms or by partisans who call for uncritical praise. Apply sober, principled assessment rather than joining in collective exaltation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not redefine criticism to please practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'alter my definition of criticism, in order to meet the requirements of a number of practising English critics' — i.e., do not let criticism itself be made to serve parochial or commercial tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist pressures to lower standards or change the critic's aims simply to conform to what working critics, markets, or audiences expect; preserve the critic's higher purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the critic's right tone and temper
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should adopt the right 'tone and temper of mind' — sincere, simple, flexible, ardent, ever widening its knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and display personal qualities (sincerity, simplicity, ardour, intellectual flexibility) in critical writing; these virtues shape both method and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to establish a current of fresh and true ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic's law-of-being is to 'learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world, and thus to establish a current of fresh and true ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to influence the intellectual milieu by introducing and circulating substantial, accurate ideas rather than merely reporting trends; the critic is civic/intellectual carrier of ideas for cultural improvement.
